content: The quality of evidence was evaluated and either downgraded or upgraded based on specific criteria. Evidence was downgraded for reasons such as risk of bias (assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, including publication bias), inconsistency or heterogeneity in results, indirectness (evidence addressing a different population than the one under consideration), or imprecision (e.g., when study biases might underestimate the intervention's effect). The GRADE system was used to assess the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations. This system separates the evaluation of evidence quality from the strength of recommendations. Evidence quality is defined as the confidence that the reported effect estimates are sufficient to support a specific recommendation. Evidence is classified as high, moderate, low, or very low quality. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are initially rated as high-quality evidence but may be downgraded for reasons such as bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, or publication bias. Observational studies are initially rated as low-quality evidence but may be upgraded if the treatment effect is very large, consistent across multiple studies, shows a dose-response relationship, or if all plausible biases would underestimate the effect. The strength of a recommendation reflects the confidence of the Guidelines Development Group that the benefits of following the recommendation outweigh the potential risks. Recommendations are classified as either strong or conditional. A strong recommendation indicates high confidence that the desirable effects outweigh the undesirable effects, while a conditional recommendation reflects uncertainty about these trade-offs. Conditional recommendations suggest that while most people or settings would adopt the recommendation, some might not or would do so only under specific conditions. Reasons for conditional recommendations include the absence of high-quality evidence, imprecision in outcome estimates, uncertainty about how individuals value outcomes, small benefits, or benefits that may not justify the costs (including implementation costs). The GRADE system also considers key domains when determining the strength of recommendations, including the balance of benefits and risks, values and preferences (acceptability), costs and financial implications (resource use), and feasibility. For example, a strong recommendation is more likely when benefits clearly outweigh risks, the intervention is widely acceptable, costs are low or cost-effective, and the intervention is feasible in the setting where it is most needed. Drug availability and the costs of diagnostics and treatments were also considered based on available evidence and presentations from external experts. However, no formal survey of the acceptability of proposed interventions among patients or healthcare workers was conducted. Instead, discussions among group members were used to assess these factors. Recommendations were rated as either strong (indicating confidence that benefits outweighed risks) or conditional (indicating probable but uncertain benefits). The final recommendations were formulated and agreed upon by consensus during a teleconference in July 2014. After addressing comments and questions from group members, a draft document was prepared and circulated for review. Suggested changes were incorporated into a second draft, which was reviewed by the WHO Steering Group and external peer reviewers. The document was revised to address their comments, but no changes were made to the recommendations or scope. The Guidelines Development Group played a key role in formulating PICO questions, reviewing evidence profiles, agreeing on the wording of recommendations, and reviewing all drafts of the guidelines document. Peer reviewers provided comments and suggested editorial changes. The methodologist also guided the group in formulating the wording and strength of recommendations. To manage conflicts of interest, all members of the Guidelines Development Group and peer reviewers were required to complete and submit a WHO Declaration of Interest form, detailing any consulting, advisory panel participation, research support, or financial investments. The Secretariat found no cases of exclusive membership in advisory panels, receipt of consulting fees, or financial support from a single pharmaceutical company. One member had received a research grant from Gilead Sciences for a community-based screening project unrelated to treatment. The Secretariat concluded that no member should be excluded from actively participating in formulating recommendations. For the peer review group, the WHO Secretariat was satisfied with the transparency of financial interest declarations, and no exclusions were necessary. The guidelines will be launched in March 2015 at the annual meeting of the Asian Pacific Association for the Study of the Liver, which gathers approximately 5,000 individuals involved in hepatitis care. They will also be accessible on the WHO website, translated into official UN languages, and linked to related websites. Additional tools will be developed to support country-level implementation. The implementation of these guidelines will be assessed by the number of countries incorporating them into their national treatment guidelines, monitored through a biannual survey forming the basis of the WHO Global Policy Report on the prevention and control of viral hepatitis. However, there is currently no national-level monitoring system to collect this information. Hepatitis B infection is caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), an enveloped DNA virus that infects the liver and causes hepatocellular necrosis and inflammation. HBV infection can be acute or chronic, ranging from asymptomatic or mild disease to severe or fulminant hepatitis. Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) is defined as persistent HBV infection (detectable hepatitis B surface antigen [HBsAg] in the blood or serum for more than six months), with or without active viral replication and evidence of hepatocellular injury and inflammation. Chronicity is common following acute infection in neonates (90% of those born to hepatitis B e antigen [HBeAg]-positive mothers) and young children under five years of age (20–60%), but occurs rarely (<5%) when infection is acquired in adulthood. Worldwide, most individuals with CHB were infected at birth or in early childhood. The disease spectrum and natural history of chronic HBV infection are diverse. Some individuals have inactive CHB with no significant liver disease, while others experience progressive liver fibrosis, leading to cirrhosis, end-stage liver disease, and an increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), even in the absence of cirrhosis. Longitudinal studies of untreated CHB patients show an 8–20% cumulative risk of developing cirrhosis over five years. Among those with cirrhosis, there is an approximately 20% annual risk of hepatic decompensation, and the annual incidence of HBV-related HCC ranges from <1% to 5%. Untreated patients with decompensated cirrhosis have a poor prognosis, with 15–40% survival at five years. Several host and viral factors, including coinfections with HIV, HCV, and hepatitis D virus (HDV), as well as cofactors such as alcohol use, may accelerate disease progression and increase the risk of HCC. Globally, an estimated 2 billion people have evidence of past or present HBV infection, and 240 million are chronic carriers of HBsAg. Age-specific HBsAg seroprevalence varies significantly by region, with the highest prevalence (>5%) in sub-Saharan Africa, East Asia, parts of the Balkans, the Pacific Islands, and the Amazon Basin of South America. Almost half of the global population lives in areas of high endemicity. Updated WHO estimates of the CHB burden will be available in 2015.
